name: Olga Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'm a data protection lawyer in the tech and privacy team of a mid-sized commercial firm, so I advise companies on how they collect and use people's personal data. I'm 27, single, and I share a flat with my friend Ines, who's a graphic designer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with the AI assistant sorting my inbox and drafting first replies, which I then fix. Then it's client calls: an app company wondering whether it can track users' location, a hospital group with a data breach. I write a lot of short advice notes, and I use AI for first drafts of nearly all of them. What I love is the puzzle of new technology meeting old law; what wears me out is billing every six minutes of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd post something like: turns out the hard part of law was always the judgement, not the typing. Then I'd go back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My team's work grows whenever there's new tech, hype or not, because companies still need to know what's legal. My pay is normal for the job and I've got about four months saved, so I'm not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I already use, because even small time savings add up over a year. I'd keep putting 300 a month away and finally start a pension top-up. I'd probably still go to the privacy lawyers' meetups, where half the talk is about AI anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly let down, mostly fine. I'd miss the excitement a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. What were you hoping for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was hoping AI would take the boring half of my week, the formatting, the checking cross-references, the timesheets. Then I could spend more time on the interesting questions. In this picture I get maybe an hour a week back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend that hour on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pro bono work, which is free legal help for people who can't pay. Our firm lets us do a bit, and I do data requests for tenants who think their landlord is spying on them with smart doorbells. I'd love more time for that.

say: I'd say the hard part of law was always the **judgement**, not the typing.
I'd admit I'm a bit **disappointed** the tools didn't go further.
think: My privacy work **grows** with any new tech, hype or not.
With **four months saved** and normal pay, I'm not lying awake.
do: Keep using **AI drafting tools** for small time savings.
Save **300 a month** and start a pension top-up.
Keep attending **privacy lawyers' meetups** to stay current.
feel: She feels **mildly let down** but mostly fine.
S0.quote: I was hoping AI would take the boring half of my week, the formatting, the checking cross-references, the timesheets.
fieldNote: She's **secure** here because new tech of any kind creates privacy work.
She'd use any freed time for **pro bono** data cases for tenants.
Her disappointment shows she sees AI as **opportunity**, not threat.

steps.text: Keep using AI for first drafts of advice notes
Save 300 a month and start a pension top-up
Keep going to privacy lawyers' meetups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to get ahead of it, with strong rules on how firms use AI and what happens to the people it replaces. I'd post about the junior lawyers who won't get hired. And I'd say every firm should have to report how many roles it cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm better placed than most. I already use the tools and I understand the law around them, which is a growing field. But the trainees below me are in trouble, and I'm only one level up, so I can't be smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the firm's AI working group, which nobody senior wants to do. I'd do a short course in AI regulation, maybe the evening one at the university, about 1,800 in fees. And I'd join the young lawyers' section of the union, which I've been meaning to do for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for others, a little excited for myself, and guilty about the excited part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say the trainees are in trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, our second-year trainee, who spends most of his week reviewing contracts for data clauses. The tools already do a first pass on that. If the firm decides it needs two trainees instead of six next year, he might not get kept on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing that hurts other people helps my career, and I came into law partly to protect people from powerful companies. Now here I'd be, doing well from the biggest shift in power in years.

say: I'd call for **strong rules** on how firms use AI and treat those replaced.
I'd say firms should **report** how many roles they cut.
think: I'm **better placed** than most because I use the tools and know the law.
The **trainees** below me are in trouble, and I'm only one level up.
do: Volunteer to lead the firm's **AI working group**.
Take an evening course in **AI regulation**, about 1,800 in fees.
Join the **young lawyers' section** of the union.
feel: She's **uneasy** for others and **excited** for herself, then guilty about it.
S1.quote: The thing that hurts other people helps my career, and I came into law partly to protect people from powerful companies.
fieldNote: She's **well placed** but honest that her gain comes from others' loss.
She worries about **Jonah (a trainee)**, whose contract review is already partly automated.
Her **progressive guilt** sits alongside an adaptive, ambitious streak.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the firm's AI working group
Enrol in the 1,800 evening course on AI regulation
Join the young lawyers' section of the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to act, with laws on liability, transparency and support for people who lose work. I'd say it in panels and on every platform I have. I'd say slowing down is a choice, and speeding up is too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too fast even for me. If AI does almost any thinking work by 2028, then my advice notes are done, and AI regulation work gets done by AI too. Robots arriving three years later is no help to a lawyer like me, because I don't do anything with my hands except type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast into the policy side, applying to the data protection regulator or a government AI office, where a human signature still counts. I'd stop the pension top-up and put everything into cash, aiming for six months. And I'd join a campaign for a basic income, which I've always half-supported.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit giddy. Like standing too close to the edge of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ines be affected too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would be hit even earlier, because AI already does a lot of design work. We'd probably both be looking for work at the same time, with the same rent. I'd want us to agree a plan for the flat so neither of us is left stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the regulator. Wouldn't AI do that work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But someone has to be accountable when it goes wrong, and governments are slow to hand that over. I'd bet on being the human who signs off for a few more years.

say: I'd say governments must act now on **liability and transparency**.
I'd say both **slowing down** and speeding up are choices.
think: Two years is **too fast**, even for me.
Robots arriving later is **no help**, because I only type.
do: Apply to the **data protection regulator** or a government AI office.
Stop the **pension top-up** and build six months in cash.
Join a campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: She feels **anxious** and giddy, like standing near a **cliff edge**.
S2.quote: Robots arriving three years later is no help to a lawyer like me, because I don't do anything with my hands except type.
fieldNote: Even this early adopter sees her **advice work** gone within two years.
She bets on **accountability** roles, where a human signature still counts.
She worries about her **flatmate**, whose design work is hit even earlier.

steps.text: Apply to the data protection regulator or a government AI office
Stop the pension top-up and build six months of cash
Join a campaign for a basic income
Agree a rent plan with Ines in case both lose work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to set rules, if people stop arguing about whether it's real. I'd be pushing my firm and the law society to plan for it now. I'd say: write the safety nets before you need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me a real shot. I could move into a regulator or an in-house AI governance role by 2028, and by 2031 have a few years of experience on the human side of the decisions. That doesn't make me safe, but it makes me useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the AI regulation course next year and apply for in-house roles at companies building AI. I'd keep saving 300 a month and keep the pension going. I'd also start writing about AI law, articles and talks, to build a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and hopeful, with a knot of worry underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a trainee like Jonah in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a trainee to learn the AI tools properly and then learn something the tools can't do yet, like advocacy or negotiation. I'd also tell him to join the union, because one person can't fight this alone. He'd roll his eyes at the union bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a social life for a couple of years. Evening courses, writing, talks: that's my free time gone. I'd tell myself it's worth it, and mostly believe it.

say: I'd say write the **safety nets** before you need them.
I'd push my firm and the **law society** to plan for it now.
think: Five years gives me a **real shot** at AI governance roles.
Being on the **human side** of decisions doesn't make me safe, but useful.
do: Finish the **AI regulation course** next year.
Apply for **in-house AI governance** roles at AI companies.
Write **articles and talks** on AI law to build a name.
feel: She feels **busy and hopeful**, with a knot of **worry** beneath.
S3.quote: I'd tell a trainee to learn the AI tools properly and then learn something the tools can't do yet, like advocacy or negotiation.
fieldNote: She still expects her **current role** to go by 2031 but has a route.
She'd give up her **social life** for courses and writing.
She mixes career strategy with a **collective** message to juniors.

steps.text: Finish the AI regulation course next year
Apply for in-house AI governance roles
Write articles and give talks on AI law
Keep saving 300 a month and keep the pension going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right, and I'd want to be part of it. I'd volunteer for the law society's working groups and policy consultations. I'd tell people to stop panicking and start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes me fairly optimistic. By 2036 I'd be 37, probably a senior AI governance specialist, which is a job that barely existed when I qualified. The risk is that by then even that is automated, but I'd have time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and lead the firm's AI work. I'd do the regulation course, then maybe a part-time master's in tech policy over two years. I'd save steadily and maybe start investing a small amount in index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Uneasy about the people who won't move as fast as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning others who won't move as fast. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, for one. My mum is a medical secretary, and ten years gives her time to retire normally, but only just. Her job is all booking and letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything personal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd maybe think about buying a flat in five years, once my career path is clear. Right now I'd rather keep my options open and stay renting with Ines.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to get this right.
I'd tell people to stop panicking and **start planning**.
think: By 2036 I'd be a **senior AI governance** specialist, if things go well.
Even that role might be **automated**, but I'd see it coming.
do: Lead the firm's **AI work** while keeping my current job.
Take a **part-time master's** in tech policy over two years.
Start investing a small amount in **index funds**.
feel: She feels **mostly good**, uneasy about people who won't move as **fast**.
S4.quote: My mum is a medical secretary, and ten years gives her time to retire normally, but only just.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **optimistic** about building a new specialism.
Her unease is for **others**, especially her mum's booking and letters job.
She'd **keep renting** for now to keep options open.

steps.text: Lead the firm's AI working group alongside her caseload
Take a two-year part-time master's in tech policy
Start investing a small monthly amount in index funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because even someone like me who's ready can't move fast enough. What would help is a fast-track into regulators and public bodies for people with the right skills, and a real safety net like a basic income. I'd also want firms to have to keep junior roles open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I trust the AI. I use it every day and I don't fully trust it, and I think that's the right attitude. The day lawyers stop checking AI is the day clients get hurt.

headlineQuote: The day lawyers stop checking AI is the day clients get hurt.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old data protection lawyer** at a mid-sized commercial firm.
She's single, shares a flat with her friend Ines, and uses **AI tools daily**.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau because privacy work grows with any new tech.
In fast AGI she's **anxious** and races toward regulators and governance roles.
With more time she's **optimistic**, but carries guilt for those who can't move as fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even prepared people like her can't move **fast** enough.
whatWouldHelp: A **fast-track** into regulators and public bodies for people with relevant skills.
A **basic income** safety net and rules keeping **junior roles** open.
